content: Consuming a diet rich in fiber can help soften stools and make them easier to pass, thereby reducing the strain on hemorrhoids caused by excessive straining during bowel movements. Fiber itself is not digested in the gastrointestinal tract, but it plays a crucial role in improving digestion and preventing constipation. Excellent sources of dietary fiber include fruits, vegetables, and whole grains. However, the average American consumes only about 15 grams of fiber daily, which is significantly lower than the recommended intake of 25 grams per day for women and 38 grams per day for men, as advised by the American Dietetic Association. If dietary fiber intake is insufficient, bulk stool softeners or fiber supplements, such as psyllium (Metamucil) or methylcellulose (Citrucel), may be beneficial in managing hemorrhoids. For pain relief associated with complicated hemorrhoids, a 5% lidocaine ointment can be applied topically. Lidocaine works by blocking sodium channels in sensory nerve endings, thereby inhibiting the transmission of pain signals. Topical anti-inflammatory agents, often combined with cortisone, can be used to reduce inflammation and decrease the size of hemorrhoids. However, cortisone-containing products should not be used for more than one month, as prolonged use may suppress local immune responses and lead to the formation of skin tags. Sitz baths, which involve soaking the anal area in warm water, can be effective in relieving itching (pruritus) associated with hemorrhoids. Hydroxyethylrutoside, a venotonic agent, can improve the tone of rectal veins, enhance venous and lymphatic flow, and thereby alleviate symptoms and reduce the likelihood of bleeding. Nitroglycerin, applied locally, can help relieve anal sphincter spasms that contribute to hemorrhoidal pain. Hemorrhoids can be classified as either internal or external. Internal hemorrhoids are located above the dentate line and result from the dilation of the superior hemorrhoidal plexus. The connective tissue overlying this plexus is innervated by visceral nerves, making internal hemorrhoids generally insensitive to pain. In contrast, external hemorrhoids are located below the dentate line and arise from the dilation of the inferior hemorrhoidal plexus. The development of both types of hemorrhoids begins with a weakening of the surrounding connective tissue and vein walls. Additionally, increased tone of the internal anal sphincter can press feces against the hemorrhoids, reducing venous return and worsening symptoms. The arteriovenous anastomosis may also play a role in hemorrhoid formation, as evidenced by the improvement of some hemorrhoids following ligation of the connecting arteries. The redundant, bulging mucosa in hemorrhoids is prone to injury, leading to bleeding. The blood is typically bright red, reflecting its high oxygen content due to the proximity of the arteriovenous anastomosis. Chronic constipation can irritate hemorrhoids due to the passage of hard stools. Excessive consumption of dairy products, such as cheese, can lead to an overproduction of lactic acid in the stool, which may also cause irritation. Reducing the intake of such foods can provide relief. A deficiency in vitamin E is another potential contributing factor. Consuming probiotic-rich foods, such as yogurt with active cultures, or increasing fruit intake can help maintain normal gut function and prevent hemorrhoidal flare-ups. The use of sitting toilets, as opposed to squatting, has been implicated in the development of hemorrhoids. This hypothesis is supported by the low incidence of hemorrhoids in populations that use squat toilets. In 1987, Dr. Berko Sikirov conducted a study in which hemorrhoid sufferers switched to squat toilets. Of the 20 participants, 18 experienced complete relief from symptoms, including pain and bleeding, with no recurrence even 30 months after the study concluded. However, no follow-up studies have been published, and the American Society of Colon & Rectal Surgeons has not issued any recommendations regarding the therapeutic benefits of squatting.
